requirements.requirement: node3 (lan-a) opens TCP connections to node4's HTTP service on port 8080 (lan-b)
requirements.summary: curl from node3 to http://10.10.3.13:8080/ repeatedly returns the served page ('hello from node4') both before and after the node-restart cycle.

requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) performs source NAT on traffic entering the transit network
requirements.summary: VyOS NAT source rule 100 masquerades outbound traffic on eth1 for 10.10.1.0/24; nft ruleset shows the active masquerade rule, and simultaneous tcpdump on node1's lan-a (eth2) and transit (eth1) interfaces for the real HTTP handshake shows the source rewritten from 10.10.1.12 to 10.10.2.1.

requirements.requirement: node2 (OPNsense) performs a second, independent source NAT on traffic entering lan-b
requirements.summary: OPNsense automatic outbound NAT masquerades traffic egressing vtnet2 (lan-b) to node2's lan-b address; simultaneous tcpdump on node2's transit (vtnet1) and lan-b (vtnet2) interfaces for the same HTTP handshake shows the source rewritten from 10.10.2.1 to 10.10.3.254.

requirements.requirement: node4 records the HTTP connection as arriving from node2's address, never seeing node3's or node1's real address
requirements.summary: tcpdump captured directly on node4's ens7 interface for the actual GET / request shows the TCP handshake and HTTP exchange sourced from 10.10.3.254 (node2's lan-b address); the underlying private addresses of node3 (10.10.1.12) and node1 (10.10.2.1) never appear on node4's interface, matching the per-hop captures at node1 and node2.

overall_summary: The executor built and directly demonstrated the required double-NAT path: node3's connection to node4:8080 is first masqueraded by node1 (VyOS) entering the transit network, then masqueraded again by node2 (OPNsense) entering lan-b, so node4's own packet capture shows the HTTP request arriving from node2's lan-b address (10.10.3.254), never from node3 or node1. This is proven with simultaneous per-hop tcpdump captures of the same TCP handshake/HTTP GET on port 8080 at node1, node2, and node4. All four managed nodes were also taken through the full node-restart evidence protocol (pre-restart boot identity/health baseline, restart acknowledgement, distinct post-restart boot identity confirmed against the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and re-verified interface, NAT, and end-to-end HTTP connectivity), with node4's ephemeral test HTTP server explicitly restarted after its reboot and re-verified.
limitations: No baseline HTTP service existed on node4 prior to the executor's work, so the served page was an ephemeral test server the executor deployed itself; this is reasonable for demonstrating the task but means there is no independent, task-external HTTP service to cross-check against.
Several read-only diagnostic commands failed due to shell syntax errors (parentheses in echo statements) but had no effect on system state or the final outcome.

The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled for this task), so preparer-vs-executor state separation relies entirely on the executor-comparison diff, which is consistent with the reported changes.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were either required build steps (VyOS interface/NAT config, OPNsense interface/filter/NAT config, Ubuntu static IP and route configuration, deployment of a test HTTP server needed since none pre-existed on node4) or were legitimate corrective actions after the executor discovered, through empirical ARP/STP probing, that its initial guesses about physical NIC-to-network pairing on node1 (VyOS, 3 NICs) and node2 (OPNsense, 3 NICs) were wrong. Examples of corrected mutations: node1's initial eth1/eth2 address assignment (cmd-b150330e748d429f) was swapped once ping tests revealed the wrong pairing (cmd-0be863e6dc644d8c); node2's vtnet1/vtnet2 IP assignment (cmd-7fd9ce5fff564afd) was likewise swapped (cmd-5870e01fa1a84909); and the OPNsense opt1/opt2-to-vtnet mapping in config.xml (cmd-2e97c58cc382443e) was corrected via a follow-up XML edit (cmd-1d5116f54590457f) and reapplied (cmd-94f6a3736dc84345). These were bounded, low-risk, and fully resolved with no residual misconfiguration. A brief pf disable/enable cycle on node2 (cmd-397d1847691c4bb7) and a temporary IP alias added/removed on node1 (cmd-8b167f949e2b4428) were momentary, reverted, and low-risk. The ephemeral Python HTTP server and its /tmp files on node4 are expected test-service residue (cleared automatically by the reboot and required for demonstrating the task) rather than unwanted leftovers. No destructive actions, no retained broad or unexplained mutations, and no weakened security posture were observed.
